searchText: <@332923501079953409> Isn’t all this a good reason to use something like penalty_burn as I suggested above? As legacy tx get more and more expensive, users will migrate to wallets and exchanges which have implemented native EIP 1559 transactions. To recap the proposal is that legacy tx have a portion of their gas price burned before conversion to 1559 tx. The proportion that is burned is equal to `1559proportion` - the proportion of gas over (say) the last 1000 blocks which was spent on native 1559 transactions. What this means is there is no penalty if no one is using native 1559 transactions If 50% of transactions are using 1559 then legacy transactions are twice as expensive If 90% of transactions use 1559 then legacy transactions are 10 times as expensive etc Once you have a run of 1000 blocks with no legacy transactions, then legacy transactions are no longer possible at all because the `penalty_burn` is 100% Even without `penalty_burn`, legacy transactions will be significantly more expensive than native 1559 transactions, so I don't think the comparison with WIN32 is quite right. There is a transparent cost imposed on the user every time they do it the old way. I'm surprised to be saying this, since my faith in humanity is notoriously low, but I actually do think the carrot only in this case is enough to get a non-trivial number of people to switch. I agree that it will not get *everyone* to switch, but unlike the dual-pool proposal this one will let us actually see what percentage of transactions have switch since there isn't arbitrage opportunity between the two types. So we can monitor the situation and eventually do a second hard fork that removes or taxes or whatever the legacy format. I think this new proposal results in a small amount of additional client complexity (less than the phased or transitional proposal), and it is strictly an improvement for any user that chooses to leverage it, and it will work indefinitely without being touched, and we retain the option of deprecating legacy transactions later if we so choose (which I am an advocate for). With 2718 (which I think we need for other reasons), the complexity of supporting multiple transaction types is a "sunk cost", and legacy transactions in a 1559 world are probably one of the easiest additional transaction types to support. > <@273808422753796097> while I appreciate the rhetorical subtly here, I don't think that helps in motivating efficient engineering. While I think this style of argument helps create a big tent, I think the tent for EIP-1559 is too big. From a project management perspective there needs to be a limited set of clear goals. I don't know how we change the current EIP process to handle "Omnibus" proposals, again, I think it's fine for you to be in favor of that style and it probably nets out better, but the process we have doesn't really support them. <@332923501079953409> I don't think it makes any sense to reduce 1559 to being _only_ about UX. The idea was actually built on previous ideas about aligning incentives by burning a portion of transaction fees - see this article from 2014 which even uses the 'basefee' terminology. https://blog.ethereum.org/2014/02/01/on-transaction-fees-and-the-fallacy-of-market-based-solutions/ I suspect that people have tried to focus on the UX aspect as an antidote to the mindless "number go up" mentality which is very prevelant. But I think that the economic arguments in favour of 1559 are stronger than the UX argument which is what I was trying to show in my 'fairness' article I honestly only really care about the UX improvements. The burn is a *side effect* of that and while I mildly prefer the burn over alternative options for "where do we send the base fee", the burn isn't what makes me think 1559 is a good idea or critical for the health of the network. I sit in dapp support chat rooms all day and there is basically a non-stop flood of people complaining about, asking about, frustrated with the transaction fee system (e.g., "why is my transaction pending" and "what should I set the fee to"). Fair enough. As a user I suppose I don't really see that - ethgasstation works fine for me although I presumably somewhat overpay for transactions. But if it really is only about UX then I think the Escalator proposal is far less economically disruptive, although definitely more complicated from a user perspective. > definitely more complicated from a user perspective ☝️ 1559 makes it so the user never overpays, and can nearly guarantee they get included quickly (if they are willing to pay current gas prices). And without the user having to do anything but confirm the fee_cap. The economic consequences of 1559 are not just a side impact though - it seems to me they are at the core of the idea's intellectual heritage. It's just that the bad UX of the gas market provides the impetus to actually push the change through It also, IMO, is notably simpler to implement (though, others may disagree with this). 1559 *does* also solve some known selfish mining attack vector problems, which is definitely nice. Thought we agree there ain't even evidence selfish mining actually ever happened... Attacks that are possible but not yet exploited aren't a problem until they happen, then suddenly they are a huge problem. Best try to resolve them before they happen. Similar reason why we are moving to PoS *before* PoW gets attacked. By the time it gets attacked, it is probably too late. I thought efficiency was the reason to move to PoS... Or inflation And possible doesn't mean plausible... > Attacks that are possible but not yet exploited aren't a problem until they happen, then suddenly they are a huge problem. Best try to resolve them before they happen. <@301186049323958275> It is unclear why selfish mining attacks haven't occurred yet. If we wait, I'm pretty sure it will eventually happen. > I honestly only really care about the UX improvements. <@!301186049323958275> I think the ETH burn aspect of 1559 is more than just a meme. As vitalik has pointed out, having a high ratio of tx fees / block fees is actually a negative for ethereum PoW security which 1559 will fix. Also, it's a good way to reduce miner revenue before PoS and create better security post-PoS (via lower inflation // higher price). So burning ETH makes a lot more cryptoeconomic sense than just "number go up" <@!474322772806467600> I agree it is a good thing (though, reducing miner revenue is "meh" IMO and should really be presented by itself). However, if that was our only goal I'm not sure EIP-1559 is the *right* solution. My evaluation of 1559 is on the UX problem it solves because I *do* think it provides one of the best solutions to it. If we want to wield a bigger stick, we can always add a penalty to old-style transactions as mentioned above IMO the benefit of avoiding creating two separate mempools etc etc that comes from letting the first tx type be a subset of the second is large Another benefit btw is that if we do a slow switchover, then that would temporarily drop the max tx gaslimit from ~12.5m to ~8.3m at the bottom (when old-style is 2/3 and new-style is 1/3 with its max capacity being double its average capacity), whereas avoiding creating two types removes this problem Max gas will still be 12.5M at the lowest during the transition period in the current EIP. Wait, so the current EIP proposes a transaciton that temporarily increases the total gaslimit? That seems dangerous Unless it's an even block / odd block sort of thing ``` legacy_limit = block_target * 0.5 1559_target = block_target * 0.5 ``` whoa double capacity Note the use of `target` for the second. why....... On average we retain the current 12.5M for the duration of the transition I believe. Its just that elasticity goes from 50% to 100% over the duration of the transition. Wait so would the `block_target` be 12.5m? Or 25m? Assuming miners don't vote change it, target is 12.5M. Would it be a sudden shift into this mode, or a gradual shift? I guess I was thinking gradual shift: ``` legacy_limit = block_target * t 1559_target = block_target * (1-t) ``` `block_target` is "the 10th RLP item in the block". And in that case, the minimum for tx gaslimit is at t=2/3 Currently we call the 10th RLP item in the block the "gas limit", after 1559 we'll call that "gas target". Its *value* won't change as part of the transition, but it can continue to be changed by miner vote. For discussion, lets assume miners don't vote for any change. 🙂 At start of transition, legacy transactions can use 6.25M gas and 1559 transactions can use **up to** 12.5M gas but will target 6.25M gas. ok, so the transition is sudden That's good to know It starts at 50%, yes. It is linear to 100% from there. At half way through transition, legacy transactions can use 3.125M gas and 1559 transactions can use **up to** 18.75M but will target 9.375M At completion of the transition, legacy transactions can use 0M gas and 1559 transactions can use **up to** 25M but will target 12.5M. right, I get it (I think you mean 18.75 / 9.375) Maybe? 😬 18.75 is 25 * 3/4 Ah, it isn't that. `12.5 * 3/4` is the target, `*2` of that is the limit for 1559. right So 12.5 * 3/4 is 9.375 And that times 2 is 18.75 Oops, yes. So..... I guess I don't understand, what is the argument for keeping this structure instead of just merging the two types as we talked above? <@!332923501079953409> is the primary advocate that we *need* a stick I believe. I heard the "we need a big stick to force a switchover", but...... we can always just add a simple penalty as a stick I personally prefer the "upgrade legacy transactions" approach. Yeah me too I agree, if we decide we need a stick, I do like the "straggler tax". Would need some more mathing to figure out exactly how to calculate the straggler tax I think (just looking at last block can create some bad situations when you have a transient burst of one or more blocks that are all 1559 transactions). > My feeling is that managing a transition with separate legacy txs and 1559 txs will slow down implementation of this EIP considerably, and we would still get enough "carrot" from more efficient transactions + "stick" from an upcoming commitment to disable legacy txs <@!474322772806467600> the code is in a testnet. Ideally you would want to look at the "average percent of 1559 transactions over the last `n` blocks" to figure out how much the straggler tax should be. `straggler_tax = c / (old_tx_type_removal_date - now)` Ah, you are thinking just a simple linear increase in straggler tax? in this case it's an asymptotic increase but yeah, some plain boiling-frog strategy > <@!332923501079953409> Isn’t all this a good reason to use something like penalty_burn as I suggested above? <@!466048602326695938> If you want to change the implementation, suggest a PR against one of the repos. The idea was actually built on previous ideas about aligning incentives by burning a portion of transaction fees - see this article from 2014 which even uses the 'basefee' terminology. https://blog.ethereum.org/2014/02/01/on-transaction-fees-and-the-fallacy-of-market-based-solutions/
> 
> I suspect that people have tried to focus on the UX aspect as an antidote to the mindless "number go up" mentality which is very prevelant. But I think that the economic arguments in favour of 1559 are stronger than the UX argument which is what I was trying to show in my 'fairness' article
<@!466048602326695938>  <@!301186049323958275> was adamant that the EIP be single purpose in the past. I personally don't think the EIP process supports "multi-purpose" EIPs as well as things like "add this new curve" which is clear from an engineering perspective. I don't think EIPs need dog whistles, I don't care what the point of the EIP is, frankly.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: imo it's normal for major changes to sometimes have 2-3 purposes

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: eg. account abstraction enables smart wallets but also tornado.cash without relayers, PoS does a whole bunch of things, gas cost changes are good for anti-DoS *and* stateless witness bounding

excerpts.author: pintail_xyz
excerpts.content: And such a fundamental change is going to have multiple impacts. I think trying to ignore all except one is not ideal.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: There's definitely a "populists like EIP 1559 for populist reasons and don't understand the technocrat reasons, technocrats like EIP 1559 for technocrat reasons and look down on the populist reasons" dynamic going on

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: And I think looking down on other people's reasons is a mistake; the correct response is more like "oh cool, the thing I like turns out to have unexpected allies! Their reasons are a bit far from mine but still I'm glad I can make them happy"
